Elliott Schuman   Certified psychoanalyst in the practice of individual, group, couple and family psychotherapy in Manhattan and Brooklyn. He is a Professor of Psychology at Long Island University, a supervisor in the Department of Psychiatry at Mount Sinai Hospital. Dr. Schuman has published a number of papers on a variety of topics.

One critic (A. C. Bradley, 1952) in his Shakespearean Tragedy, observed that while King Lear was not Shakespeare's best play, it was surely his greatest achievement. This paradoxical observation reflects the insinuating power of the play. Indeed, few works of art, and possibly no other of Shakespeare's many works, evoke the strong feelings that King Lear does. One may ponder why this particular play is so moving.

Why does King Lear evoke such strong feelings?

Lear's royalty

Perhaps it is because of Lear's royal blood. Children—and all of us remain children in various respects throughout all of our lives—identify intimately with royalty, kings and queens, princesses and princes (the latter pair, particularly, because they have not yet been crowned with authority and responsibility). At first secretly, we consider ourselves special. If we are fortunate, we learn that we are. And learning that we are permits us eventually to see that others, actually all others, possess their own varieties of specialness.

Goodbye Ethel L. Goldwater Clevans

Robert Welber

Robert Welber

Robert Welber  

Of course, as usual, she took us by surprise

And died in the night.

No warning.

No lingering illness that we knew.

No goodbye.

Just as she wanted, not thinking of us

Or thinking too much.

A mind of her own, certainly,

But a sadness that was private and far away.

I thought I knew what it was,

But I was wrong.

Leo Schneiderman PHD

Leo Schneiderman

1631 Storrs Road
Storrs, Connecticut 06268

Leo Schneiderman   Professor at Eastern Connecticut State University. He is the Author of a recent book The Psychology of Myth, Folklore, and Religion (Nelson-Hall), and is currently completing a book titled Psychoanalysis and Literature. He was the Associate Editor of The Connecticut Review from 1969 to 1976.

The dramatic works of Eugene Ionesco, as well as his other writings, provide striking corroboration of Freud's (1917) view that excessive grief or melancholia is associated with a grievance against the loved person, as described in his classic paper Mourning and Melancholia. Freud's analysis strongly implies a narcissistic type of object-choice. There is the additional implication that the lost object has been experienced in an ambivalent way. Consequent abandonment of the lost object and a regressive move toward narcissistic identification results in anger being turned against the self. The result is depression and thoughts of death, partly as a form of self-punishment and partly as a means of revenge against the erstwhile love-object. I will try to illustrate the operation of these mechanisms in the structure of Ionesco's plays and trace their source in his relationship with his parents, particularly the father.

Ionesco's drama is a theater of the absurd in its method, but its underlying seriousness of purpose should not be ignored. To read Ionesco's memoirs Present Past Past Present (1971) or Fragments of a Journal (1968) is to recognize in Ionesco's plays the dramatic expression of profound psychological realities grounded in anguish, despair, and bitterness.

In The Bald Soprano (1950) Ionesco's characters act out their destructive and anarchic impulses using words like weapons to confound each other.

Evelyn Lief

Evelyn Lief

Evelyn Lief  

A patient who has an eating problem is often as hard to help as the schizophrenic, and indeed with the anorexic there is real danger of losing the patient before analysis has time to cure.

Marion Woodman presents, in Addiction to Perfection, very substantial knowledge as well as her intuitive understanding of the person who has an eating disorder. She describes a person who desires, yet rejects, a life driven toward the goal of perfection that she must starve herself to achieve, or that, conversely, is starving her. One person might attempt to fill up her starved self with food in place of love and armor herself in fat; another might refuse life-sustaining food to attain that perfect image that she imagines society requires for her to be loved; and yet another might first try to incorporate food/love/perfection, then be unable to stomach this murderous love (as when the bulemic vomits her food back up in the face of society).

Woodman explains the urge to overeat in the following passage:

In her preparation for the binge, she thought she was invoking the positive mother; she felt loved, secure, protected, enthroned. But even as in childhood the need for the positive mother was all too often answered by the presence of the negative mother—or a confusion of the two—so in the binge the positive mother actually turns into a witch before the binger's very eyes and in her very stomach. The eucharist begins sacred and ends demonic, thus repeating the child's experience of the mother. (p. 35)

Woodman goes further, talking in terms of food as a substitute for the feelings of love, joy, acceptance, guilt, rejection, as well as being symbolic of the destructive relationship with the mother. There are a million reasons an overeater has for eating, or an anorexic for fasting, or a bulemic for throwing up food.

The Role of Aggression in Pregnancy: A Case Study

Eleanor Davis MA

Eleanor Davis

3 Rutherford Place
New York, N.Y. 10003

Eleanor Davis   Certified psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. She is on the faculty of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, and a former Book Review Editor for this journal. She has worked in science education and as a child and family therapist at St. Dominick's Home for Children. She is currently doing research in birth psychology, working with groups of pregnant women and infertile couples.

“If I have a baby, I'll die.” This statement was made by a thirty-two year old woman, Mrs. Sally B, toward the end of her first year of analysis. Sally, who had been trying unsuccessfully to conceive a child, had come into treatment because of anxiety and depression suffered as a result of conflict between her wish to have a child and her fear of doing so.

Several months later she tearfully made another statement, “I might kill it. If I have a baby to care for, I might kill it.” This was said after Sally had conceived and spontaneously aborted a pregnancy.

With these and many similar statements, including dreams and fantasies that she reported, Sally B. expressed a fear common to every woman who seeks motherhood … the fear that her aggressive impulses would overwhelm her libidinal wish for a child and destroy both the child and herself. Although such fears are part of the normal psychological experience of pregnancy (Deutsch, 1945, Bibring, 1950, Spotnitz, 1969), the “normally mature” woman is able to integrate her aggressive and libidinal impulses in a manner that promotes the development of the pregnancy; in Sally B's case an early toxic relationship with her own mother had produced maladaptive patterns for dealing with her aggressive impulses. It is hypothesized that these patterns internalized her aggression in an unconscious resistance to having a child and were likewise expressed in the resistances she brought to analytic treatment.

Sally was the youngest of four girls born to a New England Italian Catholic family.

Estelle Borowitz

Estelle Borowitz

Estelle Borowitz  

This estimable contribution to the psychoanalytic understanding of mourning is based on 15 years of clinical research which involved Volkan in the psychoanalytic or psychoanalytically-based treatment of 150 patients from ages 16 to 58 who had become

224

“frozen” in the process of mourning. The resulting insights are gathered together in this book, which sets forth a new systematic description of complicated mourning and its underlying psychic processes, “insights that only psychoanalytic theory could have provided.”

Volkan's patients had been unable to use the normal processes of mourning either to loosen their ties to the internalized representations of their dead or to end their mourning through the construction of identifications with “selected aspects” of those representations “in a loving way” that promotes growth. In short, they had not experienced “normal” or “uncomplicated” grief. Rather, their grief had resulted in “disruptive identification with ambivalently related representations of the deceased that eventuates in a continuing internal struggle—a struggle between cherishing the self and wanting to do away with it.”

Volkan's research convinces him that such “established pathological mourning” differs from both “reactive (neurotic) depression [and] unduly protracted ‘normal’ grief reactions.” In established pathological grief, patients “typically select an inanimate object—symbolic bridge (or link) to the representation of the dead person—to use in a magical way.” Volkan calls these “linking objects,” and names similarly used phenomena “linking phenomena.” The mourner sees in these objects and phenomena elements of him- or herself as well as aspects of the representation of the dead person. Through the use of such magically infused links,

the mourner can keep alive the illusion that he has the power either to return the dead person to life or to “kill” him; that is, he has the illusion of absolute control over the psychological meeting ground that is afforded by the linking object or linking phenomena. It is on this meeting ground that the established pathological mourner seeks to restore and then finally resolve the ambivalence that characterized his relationship with the deceased in his lifetime. (p. 20)

A Portrait of Ethel L. Goldwater Clevans

Don Shapiro

Don Shapiro

Don Shapiro  

Ethel Clevans filled the emptiness in my life history the way a painter fills a canvas. Her simple technique permitted little room for evasion.

To begin with she was named she. Yes, that was how I thought of her. I had never experienced anything like her: enormous the way a mother appears to an infant, a neutral pronoun the way a stranger reveals yet conceals, with the vast potential of unexplored frontier that a special vista invokes-she.

The stranger took a proper name when, after months of considerable silence, she suddenly agreed fervently with a statement I finally found the boldness to utter: I will not relate to anyone who denies me free expression! Of course not, she said. Now I knew that she and I struggled together.

I startled, however, when she audaciously addressed my most familiar pattern of behavior: I rushed to all appointments, almost invariably arriving a bit late.

One day, months later, she greeted me with “How are we supposed to get our work done here when your lateness deprives us of time?” She was risking the impossible. What faith encouraged her to raise such an intractable issue? She became a member of my extended family, available to provide information about the world, perhaps even to help-if that should ever be possible.

Now I reported annoyance at intermittent discomfort in breathing. She had the temerity to say, again after an interval of many months, “You have the right to breathe all the time.” How I loved her and hated her for that! I wanted so to believe her, to accept my right to live.

For some years now, Masterson has been publishing his ideas on the borderline adolescent and the borderline adult. His is a well worked out developmental viewpoint (Modern Psychoanalysis, Volume II, Number 2) which sees the origin of the borderline patient's problem in the separation/individuation conflict. In this schema the intrapsychic structure of such a patient consists in a split object-relations unit and a split ego. This will have resulted from the mother's having rewarded clinging behavior and withdrawn libidinal supplies when the child made moves toward separation, a reversal of appropriate maternal signalling to a child with normal wishes for exploration and the achievement of ego autonomy. In therapy, clinging and avoidance of individuation become the principal defenses as borderline patients project their split object-relations units and split egos in frantic attempts to ward off abandonment depression. In this model, little emphasis is given to drive theory.

Suicide is not the result of a single, immediate life crisis, according to Hendin, but of a long lasting pathology with origins in

118

the early psychic history whose events are determined by sociological as well as psychological phenomena. For example, for the young, black ghetto male, violence and existence blend into one; the culture's rejection is felt in the family that individually brutalizes its young. The uncontrollable rage created by the black experience can be checked by suicide. Thus, although Hendin accepts Freud's thesis that suicide is the ultimate expression of depression caused by the turning inward of anger, he feels that Freud failed to recognize the cultural elements in suicide.

Hendin profiles suicides by sociological group: elderly white male, young urban blacks, teenagers, etc. He discusses the links between suicide and violence, homosexuality and alcoholism, using statistics, pertinent studies, case illustrations, clinical observation and psychoanalytic theory. He refers to Freud's linking of murder and suicide and argues that his thinking has been distorted by those who conclude that they are opposite types of adjustment. Behavioral scientists have made a similar error in supposing that societies deal with aggression by either homicide or suicide. Recent statistics show that in some countries both rates are either high or low; in America, both are high. People who kill others have a much higher suicide rate than the general population.

Hendin favors psychotherapy, supplemented by medication to control severe depression, as the treatment of choice for the suicidal patient. However, he warns against psychoanalysis: “Seriously suicidal patients are either too depressed, too withdrawn or too fragile to tolerate the anxiety that is generated in the psychoanalytic process.” He has in mind the confrontation and interpretations of classical analysis, which attack the depressive defense instead of resolving it gradually.

The blend of information, theory and thesis gives this book an impressive scope and depth.

By careful examination of every facet of psychodynamic psychotherapy (with special attention to psychoanalysis), B. A. Farrell tries to settle the issue between those who think very highly of it and those who disparage it. Is Freud “the Darwin of the mind” or the perpetrator of “the most stupendous intellectual confidence trick of the 20th century” (P. B. This is a collection of essays presenting six different models and treatment programs for agoraphobia. All the authors agree that exposure (placing the patient in the phobic situation) is an important part of treatment, though they disagree about the degree and manner of doing so. But exposure seems insufficient, since, despite data indicating improvement, “notable residual disability is the rule.” There is no agreement among the authors that augmented treatment produces better results, except in the case of pharmacotherapy, and there is a question of relapse rates in that case. It is suggested that the problem may be whether agoraphobia is focused upon in isolation or in relation to other neurotic symptoms, and, if the latter, how independently they each operate and respond to treatment. This intelligent, earnest, likable book could have been called Freud by a Writer. It's certainly apparent that Mahony is a professor of English and comparative literature (as well as a psychoanalyst), but probably the most interesting sections are those in which Freud's attitudes toward his writing and his readership are ever so gently teased out of his style and examined—and these passages could probably only have been written by one who has hunted over the same ground. The mental processes of a serious writer imagining and then addressing an audience are displayed, and so are the processes a thinking writer pursues to discover what he thinks—when the writer is his own audience. There is, then, the beginning of an education for an analytic writer here: though Freud's theoretical genius is presumably more valuable as an inspiration than as a model for most mortals, his writerly tact, clarity, and openness are surely not beyond aspiring to, at least. (So this book could also have been called Freud for a Writer.) In any case it's instructive and inspiring to observe Mahony the writer gamely and often triumphantly emulating these virtues of the master. Edel believes that literary biography and criticism need to examine the psychological truths in literary works. “The adaptation of psychological and psychoanalytic concepts to the study of mankind's ability to create and use myths and symbols … a study of what literature expresses of the human being who creates it,” he calls literary psychology.

Edel shows how, in the lives of Henry and William James, Thoreau, Auden, Kipling, T. S. Eliot, Hugh Walpole, Virginia Woolf, Willa Cather, James Joyce and others, the patterns of conflict and trauma, the fears, guilts, depressions and obsessions are repeated in disguised form in their writings. Vivid descriptions of these writers' personalities and characters are presented, derived from biography, journals, letters, autobiography and comments of contemporaries. All are tied together with psychoanalytic insights, weaving back and forth between fictional characters in poetry and novel and the real life experiences of their creators.

Edel explains how unconscious wishes serve as motivation for creation and how suppressed feelings in the unconscious emerge in the consciously creative forms of literature. He notes how the last stories written by Rex Stout, Edith Wharton and Arthur Conan Doyle carry implications of impending death. In each case the author died within a year of the writing.

Edel concludes that the artist uses his medium to “disguise, muffle or transform whatever deep-seated feelings press for release.” In this way the artist works through problems in his emotional life. He believes that art is created from tension and disequilibrium in the artist rather than from peace and tranquility.

Art according to Edel, has a certain relation to the more benign forms of megalomania.

The situation of myself and my sister and my mother all being involved in the same school, as we have been here at the Center, is not new; it is a repetition. Thirty years ago, my sister and I were attending the City and Country School, and my mother was teaching there. The City and Country School was founded with the interesting educational philosophy that people learn best by doing; by experiencing; by actively participating in the acquisition of knowledge and skills, rather than by passively absorbing information. The first of the three contributions which I feel my mother has made to psychoanalysis was the part she played in introducing this concept, the “progressive” educational concept, to psychoanalytic education.

Family involvement was not something that was particularly part of the City and Country philosophy. In fact, a founder of the school once suggested that children would be better off if they didn't have parents at all! Of course, a lot of teachers have felt that way. And I think a lot of analysts have felt that way too, although I think they would recognize it as a countertransference reaction. However, my mother never seemed to feel that way, or at least she never acted that way.

The second contribution which she has made is to help to introduce the idea that not only individuals, but family members, and families, can benefit from being involved in the same educational environment.

This book is primarily a compilation and upating of Kernberg's previously written articles and books. The first part (Chapters 1-6) provides the reader with a comprehensive review and historical development of object relations theory, from Klein, Bion, and Segal (the English School) through Fairbairn, Jacobson, and Mahler, and culminating in the theories of Kernberg (the American School).

Kernberg remains consistently a dual drive theorist, affirming that both love and aggression are “primary,” unlearned capacities. However, he makes clear that he does not consider “libido” and “aggression” as inborn capacities which are ready to go at birth. Rather, libido and aggression emerge as constructions from elemental predispositions. During their development they incorporate increasingly integrated systems of affect states which are concurrently combining with the object-relations of the neonatal (symbiotic) period. At some point in this earliest developmental process they reach a stage of maturity where they may properly be called psychic drive systems. The pre-history of these full blown motivational systems would seem to be as vulnerable to helpful or damaging occurrences as would any embryonic process.

In drawing attention to pathology which derives from this neonatal stage, Kernberg notes that regressions to this point define psychosis and are characterized by “idealized, ecstatic merged states, and terrifying, aggressive merged states” (p. 109).

George sat in the principal's office, scowling and flicking his middle finger continuously, blurting out an occasional “fuck” to no one in particular. Gilles de la Tourette's syndrome is a disease which afflicts mostly males. Its onset is usually during latency years and can be gradual or precipitous. A Teaching Relationship**

Ethel Clevans

Ethel Clevans

Ethel Clevans  

This study describes and analyzes a relationship between a teacher with psychoanalytic training and a group of eleven-year-olds in a progressive school. The teacher's personal analysis was of sufficient depth and duration to enable her to accept through experiential insight the basic concepts of psychoanalytic theory and practice.

A teacher may recognize and analyze her own behavior in the light of psychoanalytic concepts where the analysis helps elucidate the classroom situation. She may also guess at the unconscious or preconscious meaning of the child's dreams or fantasies, as these are told or written or painted or acted or symbolically expressed in other ways. But she remains aware that she is only guessing, since her guesses are not confirmed by the child in the special atmosphere which therapy creates. She does not communicate any of these guesses to the child. The teacher may recognize a kind of transference and her own counter-transference. The child, like the analysand with his analyst, experiences the teacher as one or both of the parents or parent-substitutes. But the transference cannot be brought to the awareness of the child, as it would be in therapy, although the teacher might analyze her own counter-transference.

The Group

The classroom group of eleven-year-olds was at first noticeably lacking in a feeling of togetherness.

Jacob Kirman   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and an Associate Professor of Psychology at Queens College of CUNY. He is a training analyst, control analyst and a faculty member at the Center for Modern Psycho-analytic Studies. He is currently the chairman of the Education and Accreditation Committee of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis.

Ever since Joseph Breuer, after witnessing Anna O. in the throes of an hysterical pregnancy, fled from her house “in a cold sweat,” and abruptly terminated his previously devoted treatment of her—leaving for a second honeymoon with his wife the next day—psychoanalysts have had reason to be concerned with the striving for and the fear of intimacy in both patient and analyst. As Breuer discovered (and as subsequent practitioners have regularly confirmed), the talking cure can arouse in one or both participants deep longings for intimacy along with the most powerful libidinal and aggressive impulses. The psychoanalytic treatment setting, in which a patient is invited to communicate his deepest feelings, memories, and thoughts to an empathic analyst over an extended period of time, is itself an intimate situation and elicits intense desires, both situational and transferential, for further closeness. Many patients since Anna O. have desired to make babies with their analysts, and longings for other kinds of intimate contact are regularly experienced. Patients want physical as well as emotional contact; they want to recreate intimate relationships from the past; they want to know the analyst as a real person, to become a lover, friend, or child; or at a more primitive level they want to merge, engulfing and being engulfed by the analyst.

On Maturity**

Ethel Clevans

Ethel Clevans

Ethel Clevans  

I have been invited to speak today on any subject I choose, and I have chosen to talk about maturity and how it develops, and a few instances of difficulties in the way to becoming mature.

An individual is emotionally mature when he functions in a way which is appropriate to his chronological age and to his physical maturation. That is, an individual can be mature or immature at any age. A pregnant woman I know was lying down and the fetus inside of her was quiet. When this expectant mother turned suddenly, her baby started kicking. The mother was delighted thinking that her baby changed its position, perhaps in an attempt to find a comfortable place again, or was even kicking in protest at the sudden jarring. This was a mature fetus.

A baby who cries is a mature baby. If its mother responds to its cry and gives it what it wants, either food, or touching or holding, or the sound of her voice, then the mother is mature.

A mature baby will in its own good time smile, turn over, sit up, walk, and talk-encouraged in the beneficent atmosphere developed by mother and child, working together. So that while the baby matures, its mother also matures, learning to become a more nurturing person.

However, sometimes a nurturing person tries to nurture the wrong person. I know a young woman, who is not yet a mother, but who is seriously seeking a husband. But she repeatedly finds herself attracted to men who are not mature enough for marriage, who are really emotional babies.

*From a talk originally given at Heed University, Hollywood, Florida; August 25, 1978.131

Introduction

Some twenty years have passed since the publication of Spotnitz's paper, The Toxoid Response (1963). The Spotnitz paper suggests a resolution of resistances by means of three factors: emotional induction, immunization, and resistance reinforcement.

In the last twenty years modern analysts have learned through their practice that their interventions aimed at the resolution of resistances are not always successful, and, indeed, these interventions may inadvertently rigidify resistances, or, in some cases, make it impossible to successfully analyze the patient. In attempts to analyze repetitive patterns such interventions that attempt to be toxoid may indeed turn out to be toxic.

The toxic response is defined in this paper as a response by the analyst that causes harm or damage, inadvertently or unintentionally, to the patient. This paper is an attempt to define and delimit this subject, namely, what causes the toxic reaction, the contraindications for treatment, the prevention, detection, and treatment of toxic responses. This paper is in keeping with the goals suggested by Spotnitz (1976) as follows:

Consistently constructive emotional interchange with our patients and the elimination of errors that are grossly contraindicated would be facilitated by the development of a science of toxipsychology, which would perform a service similar to that of toxicology in clinical medicine.

For fifty years she was a significant force in social work theory and practice. She infused her colleagues, supervisors and students with her steadfast belief in social workers as clinicians whose understanding of the unconscious, and of transference and resistance, equipped them for therapeutic goals beyond those of environmental change and supportive therapy. Her profound influence upon the field is lovingly attested to in this volume. She advocates that the supervisor facilitate the development of emotional insulation in the worker by emotional demonstrations of her own ability to face feelings—to talk about them and still maintain control. This paper also illustrates the skillful resolution of a supervisee's resistance to hearing the feelings of his patient.

There are three types of countertransference resistance which the modern psychoanalyst must resolve in order successfully to treat the schizophrenic patient. The first is the subjective type, which originates in the personal history of the psychoanalyst. Both the second and third type are induced by the patient. Introductory Observations

The object-oriented question is a technical device favored in the treatment of the preoedipal patient (Spotnitz, 1969, 1976). It is, to all appearances, relatively uncomplicated, and seems to play a largely protective role in safeguarding the patient's fragile ego from experiencing more tension than it can tolerate. If, in the process, it helps resolve resistance and fosters the development of the narcissistic transference, these appear at first glance to be serendipitous spinoffs of the analyst's ego-sheltering approach. It is the purpose of this paper, however, to demonstrate the contrary, namely, that the object-oriented question occupies a central position and exerts an influence disproportionate to its apparent simplicity on every aspect of the treatment process.

What is an object-oriented question? It is a question calculated to direct the patient's attention away from his own ego and toward objects or events external to himself. What is the man's name? What was the movie about? Would I behave like that? The analyst asks this type of question because of the emotional state of the narcissistic patient. The latter is fixated in the narcissistic phase of development where self and object are not as yet completely separated and the one is often confused with the other. The ego of such a person is unstable, shifting in outline, unsure of its functions, and insecure in relation to the external world.

A boiler from which steam cannot escape is bound to explode, and many people who seek treatment for emotional problems certainly may be seen as dangerous containers of rage. They have reached the bursting point: the pressure is more than they can bear. They aim, without knowing it consciously, to reduce the pressure of the rage they carry to tolerable levels and they seem to know that one way of achieving this aim is to give it to their analyst.

Rage, as it occurs in the analytic situation, is a communicable disease, and it is unlikely that any analyst, however experienced, well-trained and analyzed, is immune to it. Unless the analyst is equipped to deal with his counter feelings of rage, feelings that may reach intolerable levels, the outlook for favorable results in working with seriously disturbed patients is bleak. One common result of such a predicament is premature termination of treatment, often instigated by the analyst, sometimes unwittingly.

The time-honored prescription for an analyst having difficulty dealing with his countertransference feelings is to discuss these feelings with an analyst. This prescription was followed in the case presented here, but it did not provide the help needed to keep in treatment a rageful, narcissistic patient who attempted to destroy the treatment by attacking, abusing, and torturing me to a point where I could no longer tolerate the feelings he induced and I would have no choice but to get rid of him.

I could and did talk about the feelings involved—rage, hatred, murderous impulses—but the talk was intellectual, without the force and feel of strong emotions that were mine.

Freud on Emotion

The earliest origins of psychoanalysis can be traced to Freud's concepts of emotion. Freud (1895) saw Anna O.'s symptoms as originating mainly in her emotional reactions while nursing her father in his terminal illness. Anna O. could not abide her hateful feelings and thoughts, intentionally put them out of her mind, and thereupon developed a whole range of symptoms including mental confusion, severe disturbances of vision, involuntary muscular contractions, peculiarities of speech, and partial paralysis. When hypnotized by Breuer, Anna O. was able to recall the traumatic incidents and she achieved a remission of symptoms. Her reenactment and discharge of pent up emotions was termed a catharsis through abreaction, a kind of purging of traumatic feelings, and it still is prevalent today in cases of traumatic neurosis.

Freud (1925) later described Anna O.'s symptoms as “residues or reminiscences of those emotional situations [of nursing],” and said that she was relieved of symptoms when “she was induced to express in words the affective phantasy …” and did so “with a free expression of emotions” (p. 20).

Brenner's latest book, The Mind in Conflict, reflects a decline amongst traditionalists in the search for a psychosomatic understanding of mental phenomena. Freud's mind-body concepts are dismissed on the grounds that they would carry the analyst into non-analytic territory. Brenner supposes the consideration of hormonal or other somatic sources or physiologic correlates of psychic activity to be a betrayal of psychoanalysis.

Doubtless, this is the reason why this reviewer was disappointed in the expectation that this book would contain an analysis of the role of drives in mental functioning. Instead, drives are described simply as “the well-springs of human motivation … as obscure today as they were in 1933.” It is the weakness of this text that with the wealth of clinical data available to him, Brenner concludes that we cannot be sure of a dual drive theory. The most generalized objection to psychoanalysis by its critics is the statement, “psychoanalysis is unscientific.” In an attempt to defend psychoanalysis and establish at least parts of it as scientifically verifiable, Kline, in the second edition of his book, presents a rigorous analysis of research which tests the validity of Freudian theory. He dissects Freudian theory into its component propositions and identifies those which can be subjected to the Popperian scientific test of refutability. In addition, he describes those which in fact have been verified as well as those which have been tested and not refuted. The author expresses the hope that “this book will help to put psychoanalysis back among the sciences and encourage imaginative researchers to investigate with methodological precision those areas of human thought and behavior that Freudian theory has attempted to illuminate and which behavioristic psychologies seem unwilling to study or even contemplate.”

In his first edition it was concluded that Freudian theory was not a single coherent theory but a collection of theories. Some of these theories were supported by objective quantified evidence making a sweeping rejection of Freudian theory unjustified. Notwithstanding the rigorous manner in which the data were presented and evaluated, critical comment came from Eisenck and Wilson rejecting the positive claims made on behalf of Freudian concepts. Fisher and Greenberg then published a volume in which the evidence presented by Kline was recapitaulated and supplemented by relevant published papers and theses.

In the present edition the data presented in the first edition and the data uncritically presented by Fisher and Greenberg are included with, in addition, a rigorous examination of methodological adequacy. More recent studies including new objective methods of investigation of psychoanalytic theories are described. The Freudian hypotheses examined are the empirical and specific psychoanalytic propositions.

Evelyn Abrams  

Marshall has written an important book surveying developments in the concepts of resistance, transference, and countertransference from the beginning of the century to the present. He finds bridges and connections among disparate schools of therapy and seemingly very different clinicians, and reconciles the difference between support and interpretation techniques.

Surveying the literature, the author brings order to a vast amount of material: Freud's views on resistance are reviewed, as are those of later psychoanalysts who have been concerned with defining and clarifying resistance, establishing its types and functions, and finding techniques for its resolution. Resistance is viewed from psychoanalytic and non-psychoanalytic perspectives and important similarities are noted; contributions from cognitive, linguistic and developmental psychology sources are evaluated; and finally Marshall states his own position on resistance, and gives valuable and original concepts and treatment approaches.
